newsitem.title: ITALY: Rate cut relieves Italy but recession fear remains.
newsitem.headline: Rate cut relieves Italy but recession fear remains.

text.p: The Italian government breathed a sigh of relief on Thursday after a key interest rate cut it saw as a reward for its bitter budgetary medicine but economists said sluggish growth ahead could overshadow its European hopes.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told La Repubblica the Bank of Italy's swift decision to lop 75 basis points off the discount rate late on Wednesday "gives a good thrust towards recovery" amid fears growth could be stuttering dangerously.

The new rate of 7.50 percent will lower the interest bill on Italy's huge debt pile as Prime Minister Romano Prodi bids to return the lira to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism by the year-end and to be in shape to join monetary union in 1999.

Analysts were pleasantly surprised by the timing of the cut, which came in the wake of upbeat data pointing to an inflation rate of three percent year-on-year in October, and said the lira was poised to re-enter the ERM by late November or mid-December.
"After the rate cuts in Italy and Sweden, I get the gut feeling of a more advanced state of negotiations to get the lira back in," said Marco Pianelli, economist at Nomura in London.

"If we have agreement of the level with France and Germany, I think Ciampi may change his mind and seek re-entry before approval of the budget." He and many other analysts believe the central parity for the lira should be around 1,000 to the mark.
The Italian currency was trading at around 1,005 against the mark on Thursday.

Prodi's hotly-contested 1997 austerity budget, which is intended to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit, is scheduled to finish its passage through the lower Chamber of Deputies in mid-November.
Approval is considered easier in the upper Senate, which Prodi's centre-left coalition controls.

But analysts saw no let-up in Italy's struggle to keep a lid on wage rises and spending into next year and said that without a political fudge, Italy's chances of being a founder member of Economic and Monetary Union from the outset were slim.

"The main feature is convergence (with other European economies)," said Mario Seghelini, economist at Deutsche Bank, anticipating that Italy could join a single currency a year after the advance party without serious worries.

Under the Maastricht treary on European union, countries will be judged in early 1998 on whether their economic performance in 1997 meets a series of tough targets, including limits on inflation and budget deficits.

Pio de Gregorio at NatWest Capmarkets said Prodi's fiscal belt-tightening needed to be matched by further interest rate cuts to boost the economy, and forecast a series of reductions to bring the discount rate to 6.25 percent by March next year.
"If the budgetary tightening is not counterbalanced by sufficient easing in monetary policy, then the economy goes into recession," he said.

"The most difficult period (for recession risk) is between now and the first quarter of 1997," he said, noting the "disastrous aspect" of Prodi's budget on the consumer confidence index, which fell to 106 in October from 112 in September.

Seghelini also warned the cut "could still not be enough to offset the restrictive impact of fiscal policy next year" and said he had cut his 1997 GDP growth forecast to 1.1 percent, against Prodi's goal of 2.0 percent.
De Gregorio said the biggest hurdle to further interest rate cuts was a bitter pay and contracts dispute by metalworkers.
"If there is an escalation of the metalworkers' dispute, that could put the Bank of Italy on the defensive with regard to inflation," he said. He sees 1997 inflation around 2.7 percent.
